card_quote: What matters to him: correct verdicts and references he can point students to; will notice errors. Uses 'is this true?' starters to teach research methods.
how_read: Goes straight to Rounds 3 and 4 because they are the psychology ones, reads those carefully with a pen, then goes back and works through the rest in order over a week. Checks the sources line on every page he cares about and the back-matter pages on checking and classroom use. Skims the physics and policy rounds.

w1_best.why: The coached guards, the ad and the no-control point, all in one page. I would use this with Year 13 almost as written.
Two-thirds independent, three-quarters at least once. Good for a data-reading starter.
The failed 1953 pilot is the perfect research-methods hook.
Gardner is not learning styles and he said so in 2013. Exactly the myth my students bring in.
Fisher and Mendel's too-good ratios, a clean way to talk about statistics and fraud.

w1_flat.why: The Franklin kite one: verdict and text disagree. Title is Franklin kite, in the charts round.
The goldfish one, jargon and no references. Title is the goldfish three-second memory.
Moore's law, nothing for a psychology classroom.
Maxwell's equations, outside my subject and the book does not make me care.
Fermi paradox over lunch, a pleasant read, not useful to me.

w1_review.headline: Strong psychology rounds, uneven production
w1_review.body: Rounds 3 and 4 are the best myth-busting I have seen in a trade book: the Stanford coaching, Asch, the Robbers Cave pilot and Gardner versus learning styles are right and carefully hedged. The weak points are checkable: a TRUE stamp on a page that says the opposite, a goldfish page with no references, contents page numbers that drift, and sources that are mostly encyclopedias. Bottom line: I would put it in the department library and use five or six of these as starters, but I would check each answer before I trusted it.

w2_review_first: I would say it is the best class starter I have seen for 'how do we know this?', especially the psychology rounds. But I would warn them that a couple of pages are wrong or unsourced, so do not take every stamp on trust.

w2_lost.why: The Franklin page, I had to reread it because the stamp said the opposite.
The goldfish page, lost because it read like a different book.
Skimmed through the physics, nothing I would use.
The Nixon page, outside my subject, so I just read the bottom line.

w2_read_aloud.why: The Stanford guards were coached. It makes sixth-formers sit up.
Asch's subjects mostly did not conform, which flips what they were taught.
Little Albert has no settled identity, perfect for talking about evidence.
Hawthorne output rising whatever the lighting is a staple that is shakier than the textbooks say.
Gardner and learning styles, a myth half my staffroom still believes.

w2_cut.why: The goldfish entry, no sources and the wrong register. Title is the goldfish three-second memory.
The Franklin kite entry where verdict and paragraph disagree.
The Napoleon version of Hanlon, one razor entry would do.
Second Wald entry, could be one story.

w2_book2: If the sources stay encyclopedias and a few entries contradict their own stamp, I would not put a second one on the department shelf.
